items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S4214

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the family court act and the domestic relations law,
in relation to establishing definitions for "cash medical support",
and when health insurance benefits are "reasonable in cost" and
"reasonably accessible"; to amend the civil practice law and rules, in
relation to amending the priority for deductions via an income
execution; and to repeal certain provisions of the family court act
and the domestic relations law relating thereto


 PURPOSE OF THE BILL :

This bill would enact federal mandates set forth in the final medical
support regulations for the child support enforcement program,
released by the federal Department of Health and Human Services on
July 21, 2008. The federal regulations require each state to define
when private health insurance benefits, an element of support, are
"reasonable in cost" and when such health insurance shall be
considered "reasonably accessible."

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Sections 1 and 2 of the bill would amend section 413 of the Family
Court Act (FCA) and section 240 of the Domestic Relations Law (DRL),
respectively, to define the term "cash medical support" and provide an
income-based numeric standard for determining when cash medical
support should be· ordered and the amount of each parent's
contribution. For children enrolled in State Child Health Insurance
Program (SCHIP), the portion of cash medical support attributable to
public coverage is the pro rata share of the family contribution under
the state's child health insurance plan. For children enrolled in the
Medical Assistance (MA) program, the non-custodial parent's obligation
for the portion of cash medical support attributable to public
benefits is the lesser of (1) the amount that would be required under
SCHIP using the combined income of the parents as if the child(ren)
were in a two-parent household; or, (2) the actual amount expended by
the MA program. For children enrolled in either program, the total
cash medical support obligation (including costs attributable to
public coverage or benefits and unreimbursed health care costs) shall
not exceed 5% of the non-custodial parent's income or reduce the
parent's income below the self-support reserve.

Sections 3 and 4 of the bill would amend section 416 of the FCA and
section 240 of the DRL, respectively, to define the terms "reasonable
in cost" and "reasonably accessible," to aid the court in determining
whether private health insurance benefits are available to a child.

Sections 5 and 6 of the bill would amend section 416(e)(2)(iii) of the
FCA and section 240(1)(c)(2)(iii) of the DRL These sections provide
that when private health insurance coverage is unavailable, the child
must be directed to apply for SCHIP or MA.  The current language
allowing the court to apportion the cost of any premium, family
contribution, or health expense associated with participation in such
plan or program is deleted.

Sections 7 and 8 of the bill, as noted above, would amend section
416(f) of the FCA and section 240(l)(d) of the DRL These sections
currently provide for the proration of costs between the parties where
private health insurance is ordered. The subdivisions are amended to
state that the cost of private health insurance, or the cost of any
premium, family contribution, or health expense incurred as a result
of enrollment in SCHIP or the MA program shall be deemed cash medical

support and each parent's contribution will be determined under the
amended provisions in sections 1 and 2 of this bill.

Sections 9 and 10 of the bill would amend sections 514 and 545 of the
FCA, respectively, to provide that the necessary expenses incurred by
or for the mother in connection with her pregnancy, confinement and
recovery shall be deemed a cash medical support obligation to the
father.

Section 11 of the bill would amend section 5241 (b)(2)(i) of the Civil
Practice Law and Rules (CPLR) to correct a statutory reference.

Section 12 of the bill would amend section 5241(h) of the CPLR to
revise the priority of deductions made by an employer or income payor
in response to an income execution, medical support execution or
income deduction order. Under this bill, the employer will first
deduct the amount due for current child support obligations, then the
cost of health insurance premiums, then the additional amount to
reduce child support arrears.

Section 13 of the bill would provide that the amendments will be
effective on the ninetieth day after the bill becomes law and apply to
any proceeding to establish or modify a child support obligation,
including a medical support obligation, commenced after that date.

 EXISTING LAW :

Various sections of the FCA, the DRL and the Social Services Law (SSL)
contain provisions concerning the obligation of parents to support
their children and provide procedures for the establishment of
paternity and the establishment, enforcement and modification of child
support obligations, including the cost of health insurance coverage
and other health care expenses. Section 5241 of the CPLR contains the
procedure associated with utilizing income executions and medical
support executions for support enforcement.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

In the 2008 Legislative Session, provisions similar to sections three
and four of this bill were part of S.8340, but S.8340 was not reported
from the Senate Rules Committee.

 STATEMENT IN SUPPORT :

The provision of health insurance benefits and medical support is an
important component of child support. This bill would allow New York
to comply with the federal final rule (45 CFR 302.56; 303.31)
pertaining to medical support, which requires states to define the
terms "reasonable in cost" and "reasonably accessible" in relation to
the availability of private health insurance, and also the federal
mandate to set a reasonable income-based numeric standard for
determining when cash medical support should be ordered.

Under federal, regulations, private health insurance is considered
"available" when it is reasonable in cost and reasonably accessible as
those terms are defined by a state. In the event that private health
insurance is not "available," the regulations mandate that states seek
an order for "cash medical support" until such time as private health
insurance becomes available. Additionally, the final medical support
regulations. allow states to define when it is appropriate to seek
cash medical support in addition to private health Insurance coverage.

This bill would define "cash medical support" under the child support
standards as the amount to be paid for the cost of health insurance
provided by a public entity or by a parent through employment or
otherwise, and/or for other health care costs not covered by
insurance. It sets out the method of apportioning the cost of the
different types of cash medical support, such as private health
insurance premiums, benefits provided by the SCHIP . and the MA
program, as well as health care expenses not covered by health
insurance. The bill also limits the establishment of cash medical
support obligations in support orders so that the non-custodial
parent's income will not be reduced below the self-support reserve
(135% of the federal poverty income guidelines for a single person).

This bill would adopt the federal definition of cash medical support
and provide a method for the court to determine the parties'
obligation to provide each of the three types of cash medical support.
First, if private health insurance benefits are determined by a court
to be "available" (i.e., 5% or less of the parties' gross income), the
court must order the non-custodial parent to pay his or her pro rata
share of the health insurance premium. The primary goal of these
provisions is to ensure that private health insurance is utilized when
available at reasonable cost. The use of private health insurance may
reduce the costs of health care for the child expended by the parents
and the public.

Second, if the child covered by private health insurance incurs
additional unreimbursed health care expenses, the court shall order
the non-custodial parent to pay his or her pro rata share of the
reasonable cash medical support expenses. Orders requiring the
non-custodial parent to pay his or her share of unreimbursed health
care expenses are currently a mandatory provision under the Child
Support Standards Act. The bill continues this obligation, but sets
forth a cap on periodic payment schedules and limits on the amount
ordered to be paid by individuals with private health insurance.  When
combined with the cost to the parent for private health insurance, the
total payment ordered by the court for cash medical support may not
exceed 20% of the non-custodial parent's gross income or cause his or
her income to fall below the self-support reserve.

Third, where private health insurance benefits are determined by the
court not to be "available," the custodial parent will be ordered, in
accordance with current law, to apply for SCHIP or MA. If the child is
determined eligible for SCHIP, the portion of cash medical support
associated with public coverage or benefits is the prorated share of
the family contribution under SCHIP. For children enrolled in MA
(regardless of whether it is managed care or fee-for-service), the
non-custodial parent's obligation towards the portion of cash medical
support for public coverage or benefits is the lesser of the amount
that would be required under SCHIP using the combined income of the
parents as if the child(ren) were in a two-parent household, or the
actual amount expended by the MA program. In managed care cases, the
court will order a monthly obligation for the portion of cash medical
support associated with public coverage. In fee-for-service cases, for
the portion of cash medical support associated with public coverage,
the court will order a maximum annual cash support obligation based on
the amount that would be required under SCHIP.  For children enrolled
in either program, in no case shall the total cash medical support
obligation (including the obligation for public coverage or benefits,
plus unreimbursed health care expenses) exceed 5% of the non-custodial
parent's gross income, or the difference between the non-custodial
parent's income and the self-support reserve, whichever is less.

The bill would also define two terms that are considered by courts in
determining whether private health insurance benefits are available to
a child. Private health insurance benefits must be "reasonable in
cost" and "reasonably accessible" in order to be deemed available.

The first term, "reasonable in cost," is defined in this bill to mean
that the cost of private health insurance does not exceed five percent
of the combined parental gross income. However, no benefits will be
considered "reasonable in cost" if the' cost to a parent of extending
coverage to the child(ren) would reduce the income of that parent
below the self-support reserve. In addition, upon a finding of the
court that the cost borne by a parent is unjust or inappropriate, the
presumption of cost-reasonableness may be rebutted. Pursuant to the
federal regulations, where the child(ren) will be added to existing
benefits, the "cost" to be considered in determining reasonableness is
the cost of adding the child who is the subject of the order. However,
where there is no existing coverage, the "cost" to be considered in
determining reasonableness is the difference between self-only
(individual) benefits and health insurance benefits which extend to
a11 the children who are the subject of the order.

"Reasonably accessible" is defined to mean that the child lives within
the geographic area covered by the plan or lives within forty-five
miles of services covered by the health insurance benefits or through
benefits provided under a reciprocal agreement. The presumption of
accessibility may be rebutted for good. cause shown which may include,
but is not limited to, a consideration of the special health needs of
the subject child.

In addition to complying with the federal mandate, these provisions
will improve child support orders. Currently, the courts do not have a
standard definition of reasonable cost. Different courts apply
different standards, and even calculate the cost of health insurance
differently. Greater consistency in determining whether health
insurance is available - that is, reasonable in cost and reasonably
accessible - is anticipated as a result of this bill. In addition, the
court is given flexibility to address the parties' individual
circumstances and set an order that is just and appropriate.

The bill would also clarify that the cost of private health insurance
premiums or any premium, family contribution, or health expense
associated with enrollment of a child in SCHIP or MA is cash medical
support. The proposed amendments refer the court to the Child Support
Standards Act to calculate the amount of each parties' contribution to
the cost of these expenses.

The bill would further clarify that the necessary expenses incurred by
or for the mother in connection with her pregnancy, confinement and
recovery are a cash medical support obligation to the father. Where
these expenses were paid under the MA program on the mother's behalf,
the father's liability to the social services district and the State
will be subject to the same cap and low income protections as cash
medical support for other MA expenses.

Finally, the bill amends the priorities for income withholding by an
employer or other income payor. Consistent with the goal of providing
private health insurance coverage whenever possible, deductions to
satisfy support obligations will have the following priority: (1)
current support obligations; (2) health insurance premiums; and (3)
arrears.

 BUDGET IMPLICATIONS :

Failure to pass this bill will put the State out of IV-D Plan
compliance and subject the State to elimination of federal
reimbursement.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
The bill would take effect on the ninetieth day after it becomes a law
and apply to any proceeding to establish or modify a child support
obligation, including a medical support obligation, commenced after
that date.

or for the mother in connection with her pregnancy, confinement and
recovery shall be determined deemed a cash medical support obligation
and the court shall determine the obligation of either or both to
contribute to the cost pursuant to section 413 of the FCA, the Child
Support Standards Act.

Section 11 of the bill would amend section 524(b)(2)(i) of the Civil
Practice Law and Rules (CPLR) to correct a statutory reference.

Section 12 of the bill would amend section 5241(h) of the CPLR to
revise the priority of deductions made by an employer or income payor
in response to an income execution, medical support execution or
income deduction order.  Under this bill, the employer will first
deduct the amount due for current child support obligations, then the
cost of health insurance premiums, then the additional amount to
reduce support arrears.

Section 13 of the bill would provide that the amendments would be
effective on the ninetieth day after it shall become law and apply to
any proceeding to establish or modify a child support obligation,
including a medical support obligation commenced on or after that
date.

 EXISTING LAW :
Various sections of the FCA, DRL and the Social Services Law (SSL)
contain provisions concerning the obligation of parents to support
their children and provide procedures for the establishment of
paternity and the establishment, enforcement and modification of child
support obligations, including the cost of health insurance coverage
and other health care expenses.  Section 5241 of the CPLR contains the
procedure associated with utilizing income executions and medical
support executions for support enforcement.

 JUSTIFICATION :
The provision of health insurance benefits and medical support is an
important component of child support. This bill would allow New York
to comply with the federal final rules (45 CFR 302.56; 303.31)
pertaining to medical support which requires states to define the
terms "reasonable in cost" and "reasonably accessible" in relation to
the availability of private health insurance, and also the federal
mandate to set a reasonable income-based numeric standard for
determining when cash medical support should be ordered.

Under federal regulations, private health insurance is considered
"available" when it is reasonable in cost and reasonably accessible as
those terms are defined by a state. In the event that private health
insurance is not "available", the regulations mandate that states seek
an order for "cash medical support" until such time as private health
insurance becomes available.  Additionally, the final medical support
regulations allow states to define when it is appropriate to seek cash
medical support in addition to private health insurance benefits.

This bill would define "cash medical support" under the child support
standards as the amount to be paid for the cost of health insurance
provided by a public entity or by a parent through an employer or
organization, and/or for other health care costs not covered by
insurance. It sets out the method of apportioning the cost of the
different types of cash medical support, such as private health
insurance premiums, benefits provided by the SCHIP and the MA program,
as well as health care expenses not covered by health insurance. The
bill also limits the establishment of cash medical support obligations
in support orders so that the non-custodial parent's income will not
be reduced below the self-support reserve (135% of the federal poverty
income guidelines for a single person).
This bill would adopt the federal option for the State definition of
cash medical support and provide a method for the court to determine
the parties obligation to provide each of the three types of cash
medical support. First if private health insurance benefits are
determined by a court to be "available" (i.e., the cost of securing
such benefits is 5% or less of the parties' gross income), the court
must order the non-custodial parent to pay his or her pro rata share
of the health insurance premium.  The primary goal of these provisions
is to ensure that private health health insurance is utilized when
available at reasonable cost. The use of private health insurance may
reduce the cost of health care for the child expended by the parents
and the public.

Second, if the child covered by private health insurance incurs
additional unreimbursed health care expenses, the court shall order
the non-custodial parent to pay his or her pro rata share of the
reasonable cash medical support expenses.  Orders requiring the
non-custodial parent to pay his or her share of unreimbursed health
care expenses are currently a mandatory provision under the Child
Support Standards Act. The bill continues this obligation.  When
combined with the cost to the parent for private health insurance or
public coverage, the total payment ordered by the court for cash
medical support may not cause his or her income to fall below the
self-support reserve.

Third, where private health insurance benefits are determined by the
court not to be "available," the custodial parent will be ordered, in
accordance with current law, to apply for SCHIP or MA. If the child is
determined eligible for SCRIP, the portion of cash medical support
associated with public coverage or benefits is the prorated share of
the family contribution under SCHIP. For children, enrolled in MA
(regardless of whether it is managed care or fee-for-service), the
non-custodial parent's obligation towards the portion of cash medical
support for public coverage or benefits is the lesser of the amount
that would be required under SCHIP using the combined income of the
parents as if the chil(dren) were in a two parent household, or the
actual amount expended by the MA program.  In managed care cases, the
court will order a monthly obligation for the portion of cash medical
support associated with public coverage. In fee-for-service cases, for
the portion of cash medical support associated with public coverage,
the court will set forth in the order the maximum annual cash support
obligation based on the amount that would be required under SCHIP in a
two-parent household.

For children enrolled in either program, in no case shall the cash
medical support obligation for public coverage or benefits exceed 5%
of the non-custodial parent's gross income, or the difference between
the non-custodial parent's income and the self-support reserve,
whichever is less.

The bill would also define two terms that are considered by courts in
determining whether private health insurance benefits are available to
a child.  Private health  insurance benefits must be "reasonable in
cost" and "reasonably accessible" in order to be deemed available.

The first term, "reasonable in cost" is defined in this bill to mean
that the cost of premiums and deductibles for private health insurance
attributable to the child(ren) does not exceed five percent of the
combined parental gross income. However, no benefits will be
considered "reasonable in cost" if the cost to a parent of extending
coverage to the child(ren) would reduce the income of that parent
below the self support reserve. In addition, upon a finding of the
court that the cost borne by a parent is unjust or inappropriate, the
presumption of cost reasonableness may be rebutted.


Pursuant to the federal regulations, where the child(ren) will be
added to existing benefits, the "cost" to be considered in determining
reasonableness is the difference between self-only (individual)
benefits and health insurance benefits which extend to all the
children who are the subject of the order.  This would include
determining the portion of any deductible attributable to the
child(ren) which should be considered for purposes of this analysis.
Only the incremental increase in the deductible associated with adding
the child(ren) to existing coverage or, the incremental difference
between the deductible for self-only coverage and coverage extending
to the child, is to be considered.

"Reasonably accessible is defined to mean that the child lives within
the geographic area covered by the plan or lives within thirty minutes
or thirty miles of services covered by the health insurance benefits
or through benefits provided under a reciprocal agreement.  The
presumption of accessibility may be rebutted for good cause shown
which may include, but is not limited to, a consideration of the
special health needs of the subject child.

In addition to complying with the federal mandate, these provisions
will improve child support orders.  Currently, the courts do not have
a standard definition of reasonable cost. Different courts apply
different standards, and even calculate the cost of health insurance
differently. Greater consistency in determining whether health
insurance is available - that is, reasonable in cost and reasonably
accessible - is anticipated as a result of this bill.  In addition,
the court is given flexibility to address the parties' individual
circumstances and set an order that is just and appropriate.

This bill would also clarify that the cost of private health insurance
premiums or any premium, family contribution, or health expense
associated with enrollment of a child in SCRIP or MA is cash medical
support.  The proposed amendments refer the court to the Child Support
Standards Act to calculate the amount of each parties' contribution to
the cost of these expenses.

The bill would further clarify that the necessary expenses incurred by
or for the mother in connection with her pregnancy, confinement and
recovery are a cash medical support obligation to the father.  Where
these expenses were paid under the MA program on the mother's behalf,
the father's liability to the social services district and the State
will be subject to the same cap and low income protections as cash
medical support for other MA expenses.

Finally, the bill amends the priorities for income withholding by an
employer or other income payor.  Consistent with the goal of providing
private health insurance benefits whenever possible, deductions to
satisfy support obligations will have the following priority: (1)
current support obligations; (2) health insurance premiums; (3)
arrears.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
In the 2008 Legislative Session, provisions similar to sections three
and four of this bill were part of S.8340, but S.8340 was not reported
from the Senate Rules Committee.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS :
Failure to pass this bill will put the State out of IV-D Plan
compliance and subject the State to elimination of federal
reimbursement.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
The bill would take effect on the ninetieth day after it shall become
law and apply to any proceeding to establish or modify a child support
obligation including a medical support obligation, commenced on or
after that date.

summary: Establishes definitions for "cash medical support", "reasonable in cost" and "reasonably accessible"; amends the priority for deductions via an income execution.
